claims.claim_text: The piece asks who can read encrypted messages (title framing).
claims.evidence_quote: the real question is that in theory, and in practice, can Facebook access the content of your WhatsApp messages or not
claims.reasoning: Title compresses the essay's central question; same meaning.

claims.claim_text: Encryption excludes providers only when clients hold keys; WhatsApp escrows, Proton needs trust, Signal minimizes.
claims.evidence_quote: With WhatsApp, you're trusting Meta's entire server infrastructure. With Proton, you're trusting they won't serve malicious code. With Signal ... much smaller
claims.reasoning: Summary synthesis of the three trust surfaces is directly supported by the conclusion.

claims.claim_text: End-to-end encryption can mean several practical things beyond device-to-device ciphertext.
claims.evidence_quote: they could mean several things in practical terms ... encrypted on sender's device and then decrypted on receiver's device
claims.reasoning: Several-meanings claim plus the device-to-device definition match.

claims.claim_text: The real goal is excluding the provider, though metadata like contacts and timing still leaks.
claims.evidence_quote: one wants E2EE so that no one can access the data ... in particular the provider ... they know your network, the frequency and amount of communication, times
claims.reasoning: Provider-exclusion goal and metadata leakage (network/contacts, frequency, times) match; contacts paraphrases network without changing meaning.

claims.claim_text: Meta likely accesses WhatsApp content given closed source, ad-data sharing, and past plaintext failures.
claims.evidence_quote: you can almost be certain that they can, and they do access them ... app is not open source ... 2021 privacy policy changes ... storing hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext
claims.reasoning: Weaker likely phrasing is entailed by the stronger almost-certain verdict; all three cited grounds are stated.

claims.claim_text: History portability without manual key transfer betrays server key access (smoking gun).
claims.evidence_quote: a smoking gun is whether the platform/app is able to backup your data. Whether you can access your history across devices without manually linking them
claims.reasoning: Smoking-gun test reproduced with identical meaning.

claims.claim_text: Signal forces manual key copy; any server-touchable key is like public copies.
claims.evidence_quote: This is what happens in Signal ... copy the key from your original device ... if at any time, Facebook has access to it, it is as if you've locked your door and left a copy at the local farmers market billboard
claims.reasoning: Signal manual-copy requirement and the billboard analogy match.

claims.claim_text: The WhatsApp server stores encrypted history and maps accounts to device identities.
claims.evidence_quote: the server stores encrypted message history and maintains mappings between your account and all your device identities
claims.reasoning: Near-verbatim match.

claims.claim_text: Server-authenticated new devices receive decryption keys and rogue devices could hide from lists.
claims.evidence_quote: the server authenticates it and provides it with the keys needed to decrypt ... could theoretically authenticate a device that isn't actually yours ... hide a rogue device from your device list
claims.reasoning: Key-granting plus hidden-rogue-device risk match directly.

claims.claim_text: Proton generates browser-side keys then stores them server-side encrypted under the user password.
claims.evidence_quote: your private key is generated in your browser, then encrypted with your password using bcrypt and AES-256 before being sent to their servers
claims.reasoning: Generation location, server storage, and password-encryption match; omitting algorithm names does not falsify.

claims.claim_text: Login flow: bcrypt-hash authenticates, the server returns the encrypted key, and the browser decrypts locally (as reported).
claims.evidence_quote: Your browser hashes the password using bcrypt ... sent to Proton to authenticate ... server sends your encrypted private key back ... uses your original password to decrypt
claims.reasoning: All three flow steps match the sourced six-step flow; reported tag is appropriate hedging.

claims.claim_text: Hashing authenticates one-way while encryption reversibly protects the private key.
claims.evidence_quote: Hashing (used for authentication): A one-way function ... Encryption (used for your private key): A two-way function
claims.reasoning: One-way versus two-way distinction matches.

claims.claim_text: Proton could serve malicious client code capturing passwords, then decrypt stored keys.
claims.evidence_quote: Proton could serve you malicious client code ... that captures your actual password ... if they capture your password, they can decrypt it
claims.reasoning: Vulnerability plus decryption consequence match.

claims.claim_text: Open source helps only if served code matches, stays honest, and infrastructure stays clean.
claims.evidence_quote: you still have to trust that: The code they're actually serving matches the open-source code ... won't be compelled ... hasn't been compromised
claims.reasoning: All three trust conditions match.

claims.claim_text: Unlike WhatsApp, Proton must first compromise the client to steal passwords.
claims.evidence_quote: The crucial difference from WhatsApp is that Proton doesn't have direct access ... they'd need to actively compromise the client ... WhatsApp's architecture doesn't even require that step
claims.reasoning: Contrast matches the stated crucial difference.

claims.claim_text: Signal stores history on-device, deleting server copies after delivery.
claims.evidence_quote: message history is stored only on your device and deleted from Signal's servers after delivery
claims.reasoning: On-device storage plus post-delivery deletion match.

claims.claim_text: Migration needs physical backup plus passphrase, device transfer, or an unseen recovery key.
claims.evidence_quote: Manual local backup (Android) ... 30-digit passphrase ... Direct device-to-device transfer ... 64-character recovery key that Signal never sees
claims.reasoning: All three options stated; omitting the 30-digit and 64-char figures withholds detail without asserting anything false.

claims.claim_text: Signal servers cannot grant history access; recovery keys stay client-side and unrecoverable.
claims.evidence_quote: Signal's servers are never in a position to grant access ... recovery key stays on your device - Signal literally cannot decrypt ... cannot help you recover them
claims.reasoning: No-grant plus client-side unrecoverable keys match.

claims.claim_text: Password handling adds another unverifiable layer beneath the encryption architecture.
claims.evidence_quote: But there's another layer to this. Even if we trust the encryption architecture, how do we know companies don't store your password in plaintext
claims.reasoning: Second-layer framing matches the sourced section.

claims.claim_text: Client hashing is verifiable in open source; server behavior after arrival is not.
claims.evidence_quote: You can verify what the client does (if it's open source) ... But you cannot verify what happens on the server after your password arrives
claims.reasoning: Verifiable-client versus unverifiable-server contrast matches.

claims.claim_text: Facebook logged hundreds of millions of plaintext passwords, Adobe hints leaked, and small services are worse (as reported).
claims.evidence_quote: Facebook disclosed in 2019 that they'd been logging hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext ... Adobe's 2013 breach revealed they stored password hints in plaintext. Many smaller services store passwords in plaintext or use weak hashing
claims.reasoning: All three examples with the hundreds-of-millions scale match; reported tag is apt.

claims.claim_text: Proton password-reset data loss suggests honest design but proves nothing about capability.
claims.evidence_quote: if you reset your password via email/SMS recovery, you lose access to all your old encrypted emails. This suggests they genuinely can't decrypt ... But even this isn't proof
claims.reasoning: Reset-loss evidence plus not-proof qualifier match.

claims.claim_text: Without client crypto guarantees, users trust reputation, jurisdiction, model, and history.
claims.evidence_quote: you're trusting the company's reputation, jurisdiction, business model, and past behavior rather than having cryptographically verifiable guarantees
claims.reasoning: Four trust bases match verbatim.

claims.claim_text: Architecture sets the trust surface: Meta infrastructure, Proton client integrity, Signal key custody.
claims.evidence_quote: With WhatsApp, you're trusting Meta's entire server infrastructure. With Proton, you're trusting they won't serve malicious code. With Signal ... attack surface is much smaller
claims.reasoning: Three-way trust-surface synthesis matches.

claims.claim_text: The comparison names WhatsApp escrow, Proton password-encrypted storage, and Signal client control.
claims.evidence_quote: Server-mediated key escrow ... Password-encrypted server-side key storage ... Client-controlled keys
claims.reasoning: All three model names match the comparison table.

claims.claim_text: Nobody can verify that companies avoid plaintext password storage.
claims.evidence_quote: Short answer: We don't know for certain
claims.reasoning: Unverifiability verdict matches the stated short answer.

claims.claim_text: Verifiable means are open clients, traffic checks, and audits with published results.
claims.evidence_quote: Open-source clients ... Network traffic inspection ... Security audits ... with published results
claims.reasoning: All three verifiable means match.

claims.claim_text: Unverifiable areas are closed server code, later changes, rogue staff, and breaches.
claims.evidence_quote: Server-side code: Almost always closed-source ... Whether they changed it later ... Rogue employees or breaches
claims.reasoning: All four unverifiable areas match.

claims.claim_text: Look for open servers, audits, and breach behavior; beware resets, obscurity, and violation history.
claims.evidence_quote: Good Signs ... Open-source server code ... Independent security audits ... Breach disclosure ... Bad Signs ... Can reset password and access old data ... Security through obscurity ... History of privacy violations
claims.reasoning: Good-sign and bad-sign lists match.

claims.claim_text: Adobe 2013 hints, Facebook 2019 plaintext logging, and small services with weak unsalted storage are the evidence.
claims.evidence_quote: Adobe (2013) ... Facebook (2019) ... logging between 200-600 million passwords in plaintext ... Many small services ... weak hashing (MD5 without salt)
claims.reasoning: Years, events, and weak-hashing detail match with exact dates.

claims.claim_text: Trust-minimizing needs client-side crypto, zero-knowledge servers, and reproducible audited builds.
claims.evidence_quote: All cryptography happens client-side ... server never sees anything that could decrypt ... Server code is open-source AND reproducibly built AND you can verify
claims.reasoning: All three conditions match.

claims.claim_text: Applied trust is WhatsApp everything, Proton hashing plus client, Signal implementation plus custody.
claims.evidence_quote: WhatsApp: Meta's entire server infrastructure ... Proton Mail: They hash your password properly ... serve malicious client code ... Signal: Much less trust required ... you won't lose your recovery key
claims.reasoning: Three-row applied-trust summary matches the sourced table.

claims.claim_text: The recommendation is client-side encryption, open everything, decentralization, and hardware security keys.
claims.evidence_quote: Security-conscious people prefer client-side encryption, open-source everything, decentralized systems that minimize trust, and hardware security keys (like YubiKey)
claims.reasoning: All four bottom-line preferences match; recommendation framing preserves meaning.

claims.claim_text: Sources document WhatsApp multi-device, Proton key storage, and Signal secure backups.
claims.evidence_quote: How WhatsApp enables multi-device capability ... How is the private key stored ... Introducing Signal Secure Backups
claims.reasoning: Sources section lists exactly these three source groups.
